event: VXE 614 (TIQUILA) flew erratically right after VTOL to fixed wing transition, then failed to transition back to VTOL with no main propulsion and descended in an orbit into the ground, destroying the aircraft.
component: XCOMM Ethernet switch U11 (Microchip KSZ8895RQX) and XCOMM 3.3 V supply
failure_mode: overvoltage on the XCOMM 3.3 V rail damaged U11 MDIXDIS, IN_PWR_SEL and LDO_O circuits, collapsing 3.3 V and 1.2 V; XCOMM 12.8 V outputs to the VTOL interface board and SA cam read about 200 mV, consistent with loss of VTOL AP power and CAN in flight
contributing: source of the overvoltage not found: candidates include 28 V hot mating without anti-spark, VTOL motor/ESC transients, ADP, lower payload harness or branch cable
Centre Wing not detected warning before launch; centre wing removed and aircraft power cycled in the field
false landed/launched states during pitch oscillations
possible left aileron servo fault early in the timeline, never confirmed
no 3.3 V overvoltage protection on XCOMM (design)

evidence.quote: The failure of the ‘U11’ device was verified. The ‘U11’ device failed due to an overvoltage condition on
The observed damage is not consistent with electrostatic discharge (ESD), and no evidence of any
It was the ethernet switch 1 IC on the Xcomm board that failed, possibly from an ESD event, processing step or other TBD.
Most notably, the 12V regulators that go to the SaCam and the Vtol Int board were reading 200mV.
Both CAN devices stop responding at the same time, indicating power fault.
Correlation with the erratic flight behavior and overall crash still in process. It is possible there is a second/corresponding failure mode we have not yet found.

team_root_cause: Possible root cause is a VTOL or VTOL ESC or in circuit wiring intermittent low resistance short condition.  27.5@20A 1.375 ohms if single phase.
disagreement: The Root Cause field names a possible VTOL, VTOL ESC or wiring intermittent low resistance short. The later teardown and lab failure analysis found the XCOMM ethernet switch U11 failed from "an overvoltage condition on the 3.3V rail", and the corrective actions target XCOMM 3.3 V protection and hot mating, so the evidence points to the XCOMM power circuit rather than a VTOL or ESC short (which may remain a candidate overvoltage source).

would_settle_it.what: final timeline correlating XCOMM failure with the erratic flight and VTOL AP power loss, and the identified overvoltage source
XCOMM and VTOL logs at the moment VTOL AP and CAN devices dropped, and 12/6 V bus transients
test per latest servo guidance to rule out a servo fault as the start of the erratic flight

attachments_read: 30911_RMA Quote to Repair VXE-614 Warranty UK MOD 250305-1 May 22, 2025.pdf.md
reasoning: Both CAN devices dropped together in the logs, pointing to a power fault on the VTOL side, and on the bench the XCOMM would not boot with its 12 V regulators to the VTOL interface board and SA cam at about 200 mV. Hi-Rel failure analysis verified U11 was damaged by overvoltage on the 3.3 V rail, not ESD or a manufacturing defect. The source of the overvoltage and the full link to the crash were not proven, so the result is narrowed to the XCOMM power circuit.
notes: SolderIronResistanceValues and IPC-TM-650 attachments relate to an ESD/EOS check of shop soldering irons, not the aircraft. Many RMA-551 scans have no text. Main investigation PPT is only on SharePoint. FDR could not be retrieved in the field. Customer report sent 2025-10; aircraft returned to customer.

event: Edge asset VXE 500 (fuel cell, heated pitot prototype) reported outside air temperature of 45 F plus in flight at 2500 ft AGL when ground temperature was 22 to 25 F.
component: ADP/ADB OAT measurement on heated pitot prototype
failure_mode: OAT sensor measured the heated air inside the pitot system instead of true outside air, reading far too warm
contributing: unreleased heated pitot prototype fitted
corrupted OAT also feeds the baro altitude estimate (VXEP-976)

evidence.quote: The aircraft reports a temperature of 45 Deg F plus in flight. This temperature is very likely incorrect due to the ground temp being 22-25 deg F.
Ensure HP does not interfere with ADB measurements, especially OAT
The OAT estimate that is used in turn to estimate baro altitude is corrupted by the temperature of the heated air in the pitot tube.

team_root_cause: Defective design of the unreleased heated Pitot.
reasoning: The reported OAT rose 20 F above ground temperature at altitude, which the crew judged physically implausible. The data review on the same flights (VXEP-976) found the ADB OAT was reading the heated air in the pitot tube, over 60 F against about 25 F on the ground. The corrective action is to thermally isolate the temperature measurement from the heater.
notes: Same flights (2025-02-02 to 02-04) as VXEP-976, VXEP-977 and VXEP-978. Prototype hardware only; tracked under VXEP-266.

event: Edge asset VXE 500 fuel cell showed an unexplained negative error code -25568 during ground warmup at idle before flight; cleared by stopping and restarting the fuel cell.
component: VSM fuel cell fault code interpretation
failure_mode: VSM passed through high-value fuel cell fault codes so values above a limit were shown as negative integers, giving an erroneous fault message
contributing: underlying fuel cell fault not confirmed: Ann Arbor team said low fuel cell temperature at idle in 22 to 30 F ambient

evidence.quote: there was a VSM error causing values exceeding a specific fault to revert to negative numbers.
This was fixed in the VSM under [MS-725] VSM update to provide fault codes in FC messages to GCSs - Jira
it seemed to be an error indicating that the fuel cell temperature had dropped too low (this was while at idle on the ground).
meaning that the AP appears to be simply passing the value through to the GCS.

team_root_cause: VSM Fault Interpretation issue, Passthrough of high decimal fault values resulted in a negative reported erroneous fault message.

would_settle_it.what: raw fuel cell fault value logged at warmup to identify the real fault behind -25568

reasoning: The Mission Systems team found the VSM displayed fuel cell fault values above a limit as negative numbers, and MS-725 shows the autopilot passes raw fault values straight to the ground software. The fix was released in the VSM. The negative display is explained; the underlying fuel cell fault was reported as low temperature at idle but not confirmed.
notes: Reading -25568 as an unsigned 16-bit value gives 39968, which the MS-725 fault matrix lists as Insufficient Fuel Flow to Fuel Cell, not a low temperature fault; this is my arithmetic, not stated by the team, and the real fault remains unconfirmed.
